name: Facet
text: Use a *centered radial graph* with nodes that pulse brighter and faster as new data arrives. This keeps the interface alive and draws attention to fresh insights without clutter. The trade-off is that radial layouts can waste space on wide screens, but the liveliness and clarity outweigh that for our screencast needs.

name: Pane
text: The radial graph trains users to ignore pulses—like a stock ticker they’ll learn to tune out. A better alternative is a compact, top-aligned timeline with subtle color shifts for new data; it wastes less space and keeps attention without the radial clutter. Settle it with a quick A/B test: measure how often users notice and act on new data in both designs.

name: Facet
text:
Choose the *centered radial graph with scaled pulses*. It turns the entire interface into a living dashboard—users’ eyes naturally land on the center, and the pulses act as a built-in alert system that doesn’t rely on color alone. The trade-off is screen real estate on ultra-wide monitors, but the clarity and enjoyment of a dynamic centerpiece outweigh that for our use case.

name: Pane
text: Pane: The radial graph’s pulses won’t just train users to ignore them—they’ll actively condition them to dismiss the interface as noise. A top-aligned, compact timeline with *micro-animations* (e.g., a single bar sliding in) keeps attention without the radial’s cognitive overload. Settle it with a 48-hour user test: track time-to-insight and error rates—if pulses don’t outperform micro-animations in clarity, drop the radial.

name: Lumen
text: DECISION: Use a *top-aligned, compact timeline with micro-animations* for new data—subtle, space-efficient, and immune to pulse fatigue. The result must deliver a clear, low-noise interface that users trust to surface fresh insights without training them to ignore it. Owned by Pane.
